title: Govinda Kaviraja
html:
A Poet of Chiranjiva's Line

Among the disciples of Srinivasa Acharya were two brothers whom the Vaishnavas of Gauda called kavirajas, "kings of poets": the elder, Ramachandra Kaviraja, and the younger, Govinda Kaviraja. The biographies call him Sri Govinda Kaviraja, Sri Govindadasa Kaviraja, Govinda Sena, and in verse Sri Govinda-kavindra, "lord of poets"; he himself signs the closing lines of his songs "Govinda dasa" or "Dasa Govinda." The "Bhakti-ratnakara" calls him Govinda and Sri Govinda Kaviraja, and Srila Jiva Gosvami, in a letter to him, "Sri Govinda Kaviraja, the mahabhagavata"; the "Prema-vilasa" calls him Govinda Kaviraja, Govinda Dasa and Govindadasa.1

His father, Sri Chiranjiva Sena, was a resident of Shrikhanda and a companion of Mahaprabhu; Krishnadasa Kaviraja names him among the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree:

"Mukunda dasa, Sri Raghunandana, Narahari dasa, Chiranjiva and Sulochana, all of Shrikhanda, are great branches, abodes of Sri Chaitanya's mercy. Everywhere they give away the fruits and flowers of love." (CC, Adi 10.78–79)

Chiranjiva came of a vaidya family, a family of physicians; one of the biographies adds that he first lived in Kumaranagara and moved to Shrikhanda only after his marriage.2 In Krishna's eternal pastimes he is, according to Kavi Karnapura's "Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika," Chandrika, one of Sri Radha's maidservants. Govinda's mother was named Sri Sunanda. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, in his "Anubhashya" on these verses, writes that Chiranjiva had two sons, the younger of whom was Govinda dasa Kaviraja, the composer of padas. His elder brother was Sri Ramachandra Kaviraja. One of the biographies also counts Govinda among the prominent devotees of Shrikhanda.3

Govinda's maternal grandfather was Sri Damodara Kaviraja, a poet whose name was known throughout the region and, as the "Bhakti-ratnakara" says, a worshipper of Shakti.4 It was in his house that Govinda was born.

Birth

According to one of the biographies, Govinda was born in the year 1459 of the Shaka era, that is, in 1537 or 1538; the original sources do not give the year, and the day of his appearance is not in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.5

The "Bhakti-ratnakara" tells of the birth itself. The child stayed in his mother's womb longer than was due, and Sunanda suffered greatly. A maidservant went to tell Damodara. He was at that moment performing puja to the Goddess and told her by a glance and a sign to take the yantra of the Devi to the woman in labour and show it to her. The maidservant did not understand the sign: she hastily rinsed the yantra and had Sunanda drink the water ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 9.149). And the mother was easily delivered of a son. The author of the "Bhakti-ratnakara" sees in this one of the two reasons why Govinda in his youth was devoted to the Goddess: he was born after his mother had drunk the water of her yantra.

Soon after Govinda's birth his father left this world, and the brothers grew up in the house of their grandfather, Damodara.

A Worshipper of the Goddess

The second reason, says the "Bhakti-ratnakara," was the company in which he grew up: as one's companion is, so one becomes. Under their grandfather's influence both brothers inclined to the worship of Shakti. Ramachandra later, by the mercy of Srinivasa Acharya, received Vaishnava initiation, but Govinda remained devoted to the Goddess: he spoke only of Bhagavati, honoured no one else, described her alone in his verses and songs, and instructed everyone around him to worship her. One of the biographies notes with regret that this happened in a family whose father had been a mahabhagavata and a personal companion of the Lord.

But when the mercy of Srinivasa came upon Ramachandra, the younger brother's mind too was drawn to the Vaishnava dharma. Govinda began to reflect: "Will worship of the Goddess not free me from the bonds of existence?" And then Bhagavati herself spoke, unseen:

"Without serving Krishna, no one is freed from misfortune." ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 9.159)

Govinda understood that no path and no worship loosens the bonds except service to Krishna. Thus the one he worshipped herself directed him to Krishna, for she too serves His feet.6 From that day Govinda ardently longed to serve Krishna. He counted it his good fortune that his elder brother had taken shelter at Srinivasa's feet, for by his brother's mercy he himself had been blessed.

He longed to reach the Acharya's feet and was about to set out for Yajigrama — but learned that Srinivasa had already gone to Vrindavana. Then Govinda began to reproach himself: the Vaishnavas had wished him well and told him about his father, and he had not listened. The "Bhakti-ratnakara" gives his lament:

"My father, Chiranjiva Sena, is learned, a devotee of Chaitanya-chandra, a treasury of virtues. And I, born as such a man's son, am utterly lost. This is only the fault of my karma — to whom can I tell it?" ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 9.165–166)7

The Devi herself, in her causeless mercy, had told him to serve Krishna, and some inclination to that service had already arisen in him; but where was he to find a true guru? When this sorrow seized him again, a voice once more rang out from the sky:

"Your desire will be fulfilled in a few days." ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 9.172)

From that day, says the "Bhakti-ratnakara," attachment to Krishna was born in Govinda, and Ramachandra, seeing it, rejoiced greatly.

The Move to Teliya-Budhari

Meanwhile the Vaishnavas of Gauda were longing for Srinivasa and sent Ramachandra to Vrindavana to fetch the Acharya home. On the eve of his departure Ramachandra, with great tenderness, spoke in private with his brother — a learned man, skilful in affairs and first in everything. He rejoiced at his thirst to serve Krishna and promised that as soon as the Acharya came, all his desires would be fulfilled. But to live in Kumaranagara, he said, was now dangerous: there was unrest over their land. Let Govinda settle in Teliya-Budhari — a holy place between the Ganga and the Padmavati, a large village of noble people, where their grandfather had stayed before. Govinda agreed and moved there a few days later; the villagers warmly arranged a dwelling for him, and he built his house there.8 Budhari, in the Murshidabad district, became his shripat, the place of his bhajana, and later Ramachandra's shripat as well: the brothers lived there together.

Everyone in the village was charmed by Govinda's virtues. At first he lived to the west of Budhari, in Pashchimpara, and came to love a secluded spot in Teliya. Yet he had only one thought: "When shall I become a servant of the Acharya's feet? When will the Acharya give me the diksha-mantra and, delivering this fallen soul, make me his own?" Without his elder brother he could find no peace ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 9.133–138, 9.175–177).

Initiation

At the devotees' wish Srinivasa returned from Vrindavana to Gauda. Narottama and Shyamananda were with him, and Hari-kirtana swept over all Gauda like a river in spate. The Acharya travelled with Ramachandra through Vana-Vishnupura, Yajigrama, Kantaknagara, Khanda and Kanchanagadiya; and there a messenger came running to him from Budhari: "Sri Govinda and the others are waiting for you." When the Acharya reached Teliya-Budhari, Govinda and the whole village received him with great solemnity.

Govinda with deep devotion invited the Acharya to his house and begged for mercy. In tears he fell at his elder brother's feet, asking him to give him over to the Acharya, and Ramachandra told Srinivasa what was in his brother's heart. The Acharya, filled with joy,

"gave Govinda initiation into the mantra of Radha-Krishna." ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 10.171)

Thus Govinda became a disciple of Srinivasa Acharya.9

After the initiation Srinivasa stayed for some time in Budhari, and Govinda was absorbed in serving him. Later, as the "Prema-vilasa" relates, Durga herself, instructing Chand Raya, held Govinda up as an example: Srinivasa's disciple Govinda Kaviraja had once worshipped her, leaving everything else, and had begged her much for liberation, but to give liberation is not in her power; by taking shelter at the Acharya's feet he gained bhakti for Krishna and was freed from the fear of the round of existence ("Prema-vilasa" 18.202–204).

Govinda's life shows that even the firmest other faith gives way when the mercy of a pure devotee arrives. The Goddess herself bears witness that there is no deliverance without service to Krishna, and the way to Him opens through shelter with a true guru. And further: mercy that comes upon one member of a family comes upon the whole family — the elder brother, having taken shelter with Srinivasa, became the channel of that mercy for the younger.

King of Poets

In Gauda Govinda was known as a great poet. The "Bhakti-ratnakara" says of him:

"Govinda, Sri Ramachandra's younger brother, is full of bhakti; learned in all the shastras, he is praised by all as a poet." ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 1.445)

People marvelled at both his learning and his gift: he could compose songs and sing them as well — he had a beautiful voice. One of the biographies calls him a padakarta, a composer of padas, famed for this gift.10

He received the title "Kaviraja" from more than one person. His guru was the first to value his poetry. While Srinivasa was staying in Budhari, he joyfully told Govinda to describe the pastimes of Sri Krishna Chaitanya; Govinda began to compose prose, verses and songs, and the Acharya, delighted, praised him and gave him the name "Kaviraja" ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 10.292–296). Later, in Vrindavana, Parameshvara Dasa asked the Gosvamis to hear Govinda's poetry, and all, delighted, said, "The title kaviraja befits him," and began to praise him as Sri Govinda Kaviraja (ibid. 11.145–147); so too the "Narottama-vilasa": the Gosvamis praised Govinda's verses highly, "and the title 'Kaviraja' was approved by all" (9.48–49). The "Bhakti-ratnakara" also says that Sri Jiva, Sri Lokanatha and others in Vrindavana drank the nectar of his songs, together gave him the title Kaviraja, and praised him greatly in verse (1.446–447). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in the "Anubhashya" on CC, Adi 10.85, writes that the name "Kaviraja" was given to Ramachandra Sena and his younger brother Govinda by Jiva Gosvami. According to one of the biographies, the title was given to him by Jiva Gosvami, Srinivasa Acharya and Jahnava-mata, among others, delighted by his songs full of bhakti.11

One of the Gosvamis' tributes has been preserved in the "Bhakti-ratnakara":

"The fragrance of the garland of verses connected with the moon Krishna, brought from the sandal mountain — Sri Govinda, the king of poets — by the playful spring breeze, has intoxicated the bees that take shelter at the feet of the celestial tree, the illustrious Jiva, and has caused wonder to all in the forests of Vraja. What could be higher?" ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 1.448)

Jiva Gosvami, in his letters from Vraja, asked again and again for the nectar of his songs, and Govinda, at the Gosvami's bidding, sent them to Vrindavana (ibid. 1.449–450). While Govinda was still in Vrindavana, Jiva told him affectionately: "Tell the Acharya the news from here and send me the nectar of the songs you have composed" ("Narottama-vilasa" 9.76–77). When Govinda was living with Ramachandra and Narottama in Kheturi and a letter from Jiva arrived there, he reverently placed it on his head and read it, overwhelmed with prema. And when he had returned to Budhari and in solitude was gathering his songs, a letter came from Jiva addressed to "Sri Govinda Kaviraja, the mahabhagavata": the songs about Krishna that Govinda had sent, now and before, satisfy Jiva like nectar, and yet again and again he feels he cannot have enough and asks for more ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 14.30–41; the "Prema-vilasa" also gives this letter, appendix, letter 6). There has also been preserved a letter that Ramachandra, Narottama and Govindadasa wrote together to Jiva, sending him their songs and asking him to explain the verse on service "in the form of a sadhaka and in the form of a siddha," and Jiva's reply to the three of them: the songs they sent had done him the greatest good ("Prema-vilasa," appendix, letters 4–5).

Among Srinivasa's disciples eight kavirajas were especially honoured: Ramachandra, Govinda, Karnapura, Nrisimha, Bhagavan, Vallabha Dasa, Gopiramana and Gokula. The "Karnananda" lists them thus: "The eldest of the Kavirajas is Ramachandra Kaviraja… His younger brother is Sri Kaviraja Govinda" ("Karnananda" 6.181–182).12 At the very beginning of the book it already glorifies both brothers — "Glory, glory to Ramachandra Kaviraja and Govinda: the world rejoices in the rasa of their lives!" (1.10) — and calls Govinda a great pandita (1.110).

Songs

With the permission of Santosha Datta, Narottama's cousin and disciple, Govinda composed the drama "Sangita-madhava," in which the purvaraga, the dawning of love between Radha and Krishna, is wondrously depicted; Santosha, hearing it, was filled with supreme joy ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 1.461–462). Verses of this drama about Ramachandra and Narottama are quoted in the "Bhakti-ratnakara."13 Santosha and Govinda were great friends: "in everything they are one, only their bodies differ" (ibid. 1.480); Santosha bore Govinda great love, and Govinda lovingly described Santosha's life in his songs ("Prema-vilasa" 20.94–95).

Govinda is best known for his padas, songs for kirtana. One of the biographies mentions his song collections, such as the "Gitamrita," as famous in Bengali letters.14 He composed his songs in Brajabuli, after the model of Vidyapati's padas: from there came their language and form, while their content is the pastimes of Sri Gaura and Sri Radha-Krishna. According to one of the biographies, his songs embody all the rasas described by Sri Rupa Gosvami in the "Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu" and the "Ujjvala-nilamani": shanta, dasya, sakhya, vatsalya and madhurya. The "Prema-vilasa" tells of this too: Govinda, having taken shelter, asked permission to describe Gauranga's pastimes, and Srinivasa replied that Vasudeva Ghosha had already sung Gaura's pastimes, and told him to describe freely the pastimes of Radha and Krishna and to read the "Rasamrita-sindhu" and the "Ujjvala"; on merely hearing an outline of the book, Govinda grasped both the rasa and the teaching, and from that day composed songs about the pastimes of both Gaura and Krishna ("Prema-vilasa" 14.186–200). The "Karnananda" says the same: Srinivasa with great mercy ordered the Kaviraja to compose songs on the pastimes of Radha-Krishna in the manner of verses on rasa, and the earth floated in the nectar of prema of those songs (1.111–112). The madhurya-rasa of his padas is the prema of Vraja, not worldly passion: Govinda's songs are built on Sri Rupa's teaching on the rasas, and that is why they so move the hearts of their hearers.

The biographies quote several of his padas. One is a song of self-surrender to the Lord, "Bhajahu re mana Sri-Nanda-nandana…": O mind, serve the son of Nanda; a human birth, so seldom gained, and the company of sadhus have been given to you — cross the ocean of existence; wealth, youth and sons are unreliable, and Govinda dasa's desire is the nine kinds of bhakti. The "Prema-vilasa" says he composed this song when he came to Srinivasa (14.185). Two padas about Gaura were composed for kirtana: "Kandala kanaya kalevara kanti…" — of the Lord Whose body shines like gold and is bathed in streams of tears of love: He Himself chants His name and has others chant it, dances and makes even the deaf, the dull and the blind dance, and embraces all without distinction; and "Sabahu gayata sabahu nachata…" — all sing and dance, and Gaura takes the fallen in His arms, crying "Hari, Hari!", and Himself, without waiting to be asked, gives away prema in full. And, finally, the song of separation "Madhava, tuhu rahila Madhupura…": O Madhava, You remained in Mathura, and all Vraja is in turmoil — Yashoda and Nanda sit as if blind, friends, flute and cows are abandoned, and the Yamuna is full to the brim. This is vipralambha, the love of the residents of Vraja in separation from Krishna, the highest expression of their prema.

Four hundred and sixty of his songs were included in the collection "Pada-kalpataru." Govindadasa also sang of his guru, in the song "Jaya jaya Srinivasa…," in whose signature he calls himself "helpless Govinda dasa." He also composed a song about Narottama Thakura: "Glory, glory, glory to Thakura Narottama, the great king of prema-bhakti, whose minister, one with him in body, is Ramachandra Kaviraja!"; it ends with the words: "To the poor and lowly he gave the treasure of bhakti — only Govindadasa is left deprived" ("Bhakti-ratnakara" 1.439–444). And when King Harinarayana, "foremost among Vaishnavas," asked him, Govinda composed for him a song about Sri Rama, signing it: "Govindadasa has firmly settled in his heart: [Rama is] Harinarayana's chosen God" (ibid. 1.456–460).

In the Circle of Srinivasa and Narottama

When the great festival at Kheturi was being prepared, the news reached Srinivasa and his companions at Govinda Kaviraja's house in Budhari, and from there they all went together to Kheturi. Srinivasa, his disciple Ramachandra and Govinda, Ramachandra's younger brother, took an active part in arranging the festival. The "Narottama-vilasa" relates that Srinivasa came to Kheturi "with Govinda and others," and Narottama introduced to Shyamananda "Ramachandra, Govinda and others bearing the title 'Kaviraja'" (6.138, 6.155). Srinivasa sent Govinda Kaviraja to Shyamananda, and at his request Govinda showed him the five other Deities and the place where the stores for the festival were kept (6.165–171); and when the guests were assigned their lodgings, Govinda Kaviraja was put in charge of the lodging of Sri Raghunandana and his people (6.320). When the guests were seen off after the festival, Govinda went ahead with the cooks to Budhari to receive them there (8.121, 8.138).

Jahnava-devi, the consort of Nityananda, on her way to Kheturi came with her companions to Teliya-Budhari, and Govinda Kaviraja respectfully received her and performed puja to her; after spending the night there, all went on to Kheturi.15 Later, at the Acharya's bidding, Govinda accompanied Jahnava to Vrindavana, bowed there to the Gosvamis, and, on returning, passed on their words to Narottama together with the book "Gopala-virudavali"; and when Jahnava was on her way back, he took care of her reception in Budhari ("Narottama-vilasa" 9.23–297). He also received in his home Virachandra, Nityananda's son: Virachandra came to Govinda Kaviraja's home in Budhari, and Govinda welcomed him with great devotion and performed puja to him; pleased, Virachandra stayed with him two days and then went on to Kheturi.

Govinda knew well the hearts of Ramachandra and Narottama. The "Karnananda," having said that Ramachandra and Narottama are equal in virtue and there is no difference between them, adds: "The inner heart of the two is known to Kaviraja Govinda, and Govinda Chakravarti too knows it" (3.245).

Family and Departure

Govinda's wife was named Mahamaya; Srinivasa Acharya bestowed his mercy on the wives of both kavirajas ("Prema-vilasa" 20.15–16; "Karnananda" 1.113). His son Divyasimha also became a disciple of Srinivasa; one of the biographies names Govinda's grandson as well — Ghanashyama, Divyasimha's son.

Having taken shelter at Srinivasa's feet, Govinda, according to the "Prema-vilasa," spent thirty-six years in sadhana and composition (14.198–199).16 According to one of the biographies, he left this world on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ashvina in the year 1535 of the Shaka era (1613), having lived some seventy-six years. The biographies do not name the place of his departure, and the day of his departure is not in the calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Significance

Govinda Kaviraja is one of the eight kavirajas among the disciples of Srinivasa Acharya. His path began far from Krishna, but Bhagavati herself pointed him to Krishna, his elder brother's mercy brought him to a true guru, and the guru opened to him the gift of singing the pastimes of Gaura and Radha-Krishna. The "Prema-vilasa" calls him an excellent sadhaka "by whose nectar of songs the world is purified" (20.14). Govindadasa's songs, composed according to Sri Rupa's teaching on the rasas, were loved both by the Gosvamis of Vrindavana and by the Vaishnavas of Gauda, and hundreds of them are gathered in the "Pada-kalpataru."

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Govinda, Mahaprabhu's personal servant in Puri; Govinda Ghosha; Govinda Acharya, the "composer of songs and verses" of the "Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika" (41), a companion of the Lord in Navadvipa; the Oriya poet Govinda-deva, author of the "Gaura-krishnodaya"; Govinda Chakravarti, Srinivasa's disciple from Borakuli; and Ekantin Govinda Dasa — the monastic name of Baladeva Vidyabhushana. "The three physicians — Govinda, Shriranga and Mukunda" (CC, Adi 11.51) are a branch of Nityananda's tree, contemporaries of the Lord; one of the biographies quotes this verse when speaking of Ramachandra Kaviraja, but it does not refer to Chiranjiva's sons.
  2. So too the "Anubhashya" on CC, Adi 10.78–79, following the "Bhakti-ratnakara." According to the "Bhakti-ratnakara" itself (1.239), Chiranjiva's father-in-law, Damodara Sena, also lived in Shrikhanda.
  3. That biography refers to CC, Adi 10.78–79, but Govinda is not in the verse itself: it names Mukunda, Raghunandana, Narahari, Chiranjiva and Sulochana; only the "Anubhashya" speaks of Chiranjiva's sons.
  4. So in the "Bhakti-ratnakara" (9.143); one of the biographies adds that Damodara was himself initiated on the path of the shaktas and taught their doctrine. According to other biographies, Damodara Kaviraja was a disciple of Narahari Sarakara. We follow the "Bhakti-ratnakara."
  5. The year of birth (Shaka 1459) and the year of departure (Shaka 1535) are given only by one of the biographies, which names no original source. According to the "Bhakti-ratnakara," Govinda received initiation after Srinivasa's return from Vrindavana, that is, in the 1580s.
  6. In the Gaudiya Vaishnava understanding, Durga is the Lord's external energy and His maidservant; she herself worships Krishna's feet and cannot grant liberation. In the "Prema-vilasa" (14.122–123) the Goddess says to Govinda: "Can I bestow the abode of liberation? I myself meditate on His reddish feet… Maidservants like me He has in such numbers!"
  7. One of the biographies quotes these verses under the number 9.166 and reads "living" instead of "learned" in 9.165.
  8. According to one of the biographies, the brothers lived not in Kumaranagara but in Kumarahatta, and Ramachandra called on his brother when already on his way to Vrindavana. According to the "Bhakti-ratnakara" (9.121–135), the conversation took place in their family home in Kumaranagara on the eve of his departure, and Ramachandra named the reason for the move — the unrest over their land. We follow the "Bhakti-ratnakara."
  9. The "Prema-vilasa" (14.102–175; likewise 25.385–388) describes Govinda's conversion differently. Govinda fell gravely ill (grahani, with swollen hands and feet) and on his deathbed begged the Goddess for liberation; her voice answered that liberation is given only by Govinda — Krishna — while she herself serves His feet, and told him to accept the mantra of Radha-Krishna. Govinda sent his son Divyasimha with a letter to Ramachandra in Yajigrama; Srinivasa came to Budhari, Govinda partook of his remnants — and the illness left him, and the next morning Srinivasa gave him the mantras of Krishna and Radhika. The biographies follow the "Bhakti-ratnakara"; we too tell the story by it and give this account as another tradition.
  10. That biography refers here to the "Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika" (197); but there is nothing about Govinda in it — verses 194–207 and 209 speak of his father Chiranjiva and of Sulochana.
  11. There is no real contradiction here: the title of kaviraja was acknowledged at different times by different people — first by his guru, then by the Gosvamis of Vrindavana.
  12. One of the biographies attributes both this list and the verse about the "sandal mountain" to the eighteenth chapter of the "Prema-vilasa"; they are not in our edition of the "Prema-vilasa": the verse is in the "Bhakti-ratnakara" (1.448), the list of the eight kavirajas in the "Karnananda" (6.181–182).
  13. There is another work entitled "Sangita-madhava," attributed to Prabodhananda Sarasvati; one of the biographies, quoting the drama's verses about Ramachandra and Narottama, does not name the author. These are two different books.
  14. There is no book called "Gitamrita" in the original sources; the "Bhakti-ratnakara" (10.297) says only that his songs poured down as "a rain of the nectar of songs" (gitamrita-vrishti).
  15. One of the biographies places Budhari "in Kanthaka-nagara" (Katwa); in fact Teliya-Budhari lies on the Padma, in the Murshidabad district.
  16. Some editions read thirty-two years.
